title: Cleaning the Oceans
summary: How plastic trash reaches the ocean, why it harms sea animals and breaks into tiny pieces, how currents gather it, and how people clean it up and keep it out of the sea.
poll: Keeping trash out of the ocean is easier than cleaning it up.

versions.title: Help the Sea
versions.text:
The sea is big and blue. It is home to fish, crabs, and whales. But the sea has a big problem. Trash!

A lot of the trash is plastic. Some is left on the beach. Some is blown by the wind. Rain can wash it to a stream. The stream takes it to the sea.

Plastic does not rot. It just breaks into bits. The bits get small, but they do not go away.

Trash can hurt sea life. A sea turtle may see a bag. It looks like a jelly. The turtle eats it and gets sick. Birds and fish eat plastic, too. Some get stuck in old nets.

The sea moves in big loops. The loops pull trash to the same spots. Some spots are huge.

People work to clean the ocean. They pick up trash on the beach. Boats scoop trash from the waves.

The best plan is to stop the trash first. Use a cloth bag. Fill a bottle you can use again. Recycle cans and plastic.

The sea helps us. We can help the sea, too!

versions.title: Cleaning the Oceans
versions.text:
The ocean covers about seven tenths of our planet. It is home to fish, whales, sea turtles, and colorful coral reefs, like those in the Red Sea. But today the ocean faces a serious problem: it is filling up with trash.

Much of this trash is plastic. Every year, millions of tons of plastic enter the ocean. Most of it starts on land as litter. Wind blows it, and rain washes it into rivers, which carry it to the sea. Old fishing nets are another source.

Plastic does not rot the way food or leaves do. Instead, sunlight and waves break it into smaller and smaller pieces. These pieces never truly disappear.

Trash can harm sea animals in many ways. A sea turtle may mistake a floating plastic bag for a jellyfish and eat it. Birds and fish swallow plastic, too. Some animals get trapped in lost fishing nets.

Ocean water flows in huge circles called currents. These currents push floating trash into the same areas, where giant garbage patches form.

Many people are working to clean the ocean. Volunteers pick up trash on beaches. Special boats collect trash from the water, and barriers catch trash in rivers.

However, the best solution is to keep trash out of the ocean. Using cloth bags and refillable bottles, and choosing to recycle, all help.

The ocean helps us every day. Now we can help it in return.

versions.title: Cleaning the Oceans: A Global Challenge
versions.text:
The ocean covers approximately seventy percent of our planet's surface. It sustains fish, whales, sea turtles, and vibrant coral reefs, such as those along the Red Sea. Today, however, the ocean confronts a serious challenge, because it is gradually accumulating enormous quantities of trash.

Much of this marine debris is plastic, and every year millions of tons of plastic enter the ocean. Most of it originates on land as litter, which wind carries and rainfall washes into rivers that transport it to the sea. Fishing nets abandoned or lost by boats represent another major source.

Plastic does not decompose the way food or leaves do. Instead, sunlight and waves gradually break it into smaller and smaller fragments, eventually producing microplastics, pieces so tiny that they are difficult to see and nearly impossible to remove. Researchers have discovered microplastics in seafood, in table salt, and even in the deepest ocean trenches.

Debris harms marine animals in numerous ways. A sea turtle may mistake a floating plastic bag for a jellyfish and swallow it, while seabirds and fish also consume plastic. Other animals become entangled in abandoned fishing nets, which continue trapping creatures for years.

Ocean water circulates in enormous rotating currents. These currents push floating trash into the same regions, where gigantic garbage patches form far from any shore. The largest, located in the Pacific Ocean between Hawaii and California, covers an area several times larger than many countries, although much of its debris consists of scattered fragments rather than a solid floating island.

Many people are working to clean the ocean. Volunteers collect trash on beaches, including along the coastline of Saudi Arabia, while specialized boats gather debris from the water and floating barriers intercept trash in rivers before it reaches the sea.

Nevertheless, prevention remains the most effective solution, because removing plastic from the vast ocean is far more difficult than keeping it out. Using cloth bags and refillable bottles, and choosing to recycle, all make a genuine difference.

The ocean benefits us daily, providing food, oxygen, and beauty, and we can now help it in return.

The ocean benefits humanity daily, providing food, oxygen, and beauty, and we can now help it in return.

versions.title: Cleaning the Oceans: A Global Challenge
versions.text:
The ocean covers approximately seventy percent of our planet's surface and sustains fish, whales, sea turtles, and vibrant coral reefs, such as those along the Red Sea. Much of this marine debris is plastic, and every year millions of tons of plastic enter the ocean. Most of it originates on land as litter, which wind carries and rainfall washes into rivers that transport it to the sea. Fishing nets that boats abandon or lose at sea are another big source of this waste.

Plastic does not decompose the way food or leaves do; instead, sunlight and waves gradually fragment it into progressively smaller pieces, eventually producing microplastics, particles so minuscule that they are difficult to detect and nearly impossible to remove. Researchers have identified microplastics in seafood, in table salt, and even in the deepest oceanic trenches, demonstrating how extensively the contamination has penetrated the global environment.

Debris harms marine animals in numerous ways: a sea turtle may mistake a floating plastic bag for a jellyfish and swallow it, while seabirds and fish also consume plastic. Other animals become entangled in abandoned fishing nets, which continue trapping creatures for years.

Ocean water circulates in enormous rotating currents, which concentrate floating trash in particular regions, where gigantic garbage patches form far from any shore. The largest, located in the Pacific Ocean between Hawaii and California, extends across an area several times larger than numerous countries, although much of its debris consists of scattered fragments rather than a solid, floating island.

Many organizations and individuals are working to clean the ocean: volunteers collect trash on beaches, including along the coastline of Saudi Arabia, while specialized vessels gather debris from the water and floating barriers intercept trash in rivers before it reaches the sea.

Nevertheless, prevention remains the most effective solution, because removing plastic from the vast ocean is considerably more difficult than keeping it out. Using cloth bags and refillable bottles, avoiding unnecessary disposable packaging, and choosing to recycle all make a real and lasting difference.

The ocean benefits humanity daily, providing food, oxygen, employment, and extraordinary beauty, and through thoughtful everyday decisions, each of us can now help it in return.

collect used things so they can be made into new things

LOW.modelAnswer: I can use a cloth bag instead of a plastic one, because that means less plastic trash ends up in rivers and the ocean. I can also choose to recycle, because recycling keeps plastic out of the ocean where it can harm turtles and other animals.

MID.prompt: Explain how a plastic bottle dropped in a city could end up in the ocean, and one way to stop it. Use the words litter and current.
checklist: I described the bottle's path from land to sea.
I explained one way to stop it.
I used details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: A plastic bottle dropped as litter in a city can be blown by the wind or washed by rain into a river, and the river's current then carries it all the way out to the ocean. One way to stop this from happening is to use refillable bottles instead of throwing plastic ones away as litter in the first place, since bottles that never become trash can never reach the sea. Floating barriers placed in rivers can also catch litter like bottles before it travels any farther toward the ocean.

HIGH.prompt: Argue whether cleanup or prevention matters more for the ocean. Use the words microplastic and prevention, and support your view with evidence.
checklist: I used microplastic and prevention correctly.
I supported my position with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I believe prevention matters more than cleanup for protecting the ocean. The article explains that plastic trash never completely disappears, because sunlight and waves only break it into smaller and smaller pieces of microplastic that spread through the water and accumulate in giant garbage patches, which makes full cleanup nearly impossible once trash is already in the sea. While volunteers and special boats can remove some visible trash, prevention methods, like using cloth bags, refillable bottles, and recycling, stop plastic from becoming litter and reaching rivers in the first place, which is far more effective than trying to clean up microplastic that can never truly be fully removed.
